column1: What is the defining structural property of a distributed system (not merely a performance characteristic)?
column2: The absence of shared memory: every node has its own address space, clock, and view of the world, making communication the only coordination mechanism, and communication takes non-zero, unbounded time.

column1: Why is there no 'global time' in a distributed system?
column2: No hardware register exists to read wall-clock time across all nodes simultaneously; every clock drifts, and NTP only corrects drift to within tens of ms (LAN) or hundreds of ms (WAN), it never eliminates it.

column1: What is the central difficulty that makes partial failure hard to handle in distributed systems?
column2: Surviving nodes cannot distinguish a crashed node from a very slow one, nor a network partition from a node outage — failure detection is inherently ambiguous.

column1: Why is a 'snapshot' of distributed state described as reconstructed rather than observed?
column2: There is no instruction that atomically reads the state of two processes on different machines, so any global state view must be assembled after the fact from independent, non-simultaneous observations.

column1: List the kernel/hardware layers a message traverses on the sending node before leaving as an Ethernet frame.
column2: Application (user space) → Syscall interface (glibc/musl) → Kernel VFS/Socket layer → TCP/IP stack (net subsystem) → NIC driver (kernel module) → Hardware NIC/DMA engine → Ethernet frame onto the wire.

column1: What data structure does the Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) use to manage runnable threads, and what metric drives selection?
column2: A red-black tree keyed on `vruntime` (virtual runtime); CFS always picks the thread with the smallest vruntime to run next, approximating fair CPU time allocation.

column1: What happens during Linux process creation at the kernel level regarding the process descriptor and address space?
column2: The kernel allocates a new `task_struct` (process descriptor) and initializes the process's virtual address space (`mm_struct`) via functions like `mm_init()` before the process can be scheduled and set to `TASK_RUNNING`.

column1: What is the difference between the page cache and the buffer cache in the Linux memory subsystem?
column2: The page cache stores recently accessed pages to reduce page faults (memory-level caching), while the buffer cache stores recently accessed data blocks to reduce disk I/O accesses (I/O-level caching).

column1: What is the function of the page table in virtual memory management?
column2: It is a data structure that maps virtual addresses to physical addresses, enabling the kernel to manage memory allocation, deallocation, and access isolation between processes.

column1: In a Raft-based consensus cluster of N nodes, what is the formula for quorum, and why is it required?
column2: Quorum Q = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1. A strict majority is required so that any two quorums (e.g., for leader election and log commitment) must overlap in at least one node, preventing split-brain and ensuring consistency.

column1: What does etcd's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) revision model guarantee?
column2: Every write produces a new, monotonically increasing revision number, allowing readers to access consistent historical snapshots and enabling watch mechanisms to detect ordered state changes without locking.

column1: Why can't surviving nodes in a distributed system simply 'wait longer' to resolve the ambiguity between a crashed node and a network partition?
column2: Because any timeout-based distinction is a heuristic, not a guarantee — asynchronous networks provide no upper bound on message delay, so no finite timeout can definitively distinguish a slow/partitioned node from a truly dead one (this underlies the FLP impossibility result).
